descriptions.ai_verbatim: Pasted the prompt into an AI chatbot and submitted its answer unchanged.
descriptions.ai_round: Asked an AI, then rounded the numbers to multiples of 5 because they looked cleaner.

descriptions.human_proportional: Split soldiers in proportion to castle points, rounding by hand.
descriptions.human_top_heavy: Ignored the cheap castles and stacked the valuable ones.
descriptions.human_all_in: Bet everything on one or two castles.
descriptions.human_plus1: Guessed what most people do and added one soldier to beat it.
descriptions.human_random: Low effort: typed numbers that roughly added up.
descriptions.human_underdog: Fought for the cheap castles everyone else ignores.

For Game 1, I guessed what most applicants would pick (proportional, even, linear and moderately top-heavy splits) and chose numbers just above the common round values on castles 3-5, plus token soldiers on castles 1-2 to beat people who leave them at zero. For Game 2, the four-player format with a payout that heavily favors first place rewards concentrating your soldiers, because spread armies rarely have the top bid against three opponents. Castles 4 and 5 together guarantee first place, so I put everything there. I used 44/56 instead of 50/50 so I win castle 5 against the most likely competing concentrated picks. All of this rests on guesses about how other applicants behave, not a provably optimal answer.

For Game 1, I used the fact that the score is average points, which makes each castle independent: you earn its value times the share of opponents you outbid. So I treated the Nash equilibrium (uniform marginals, mean equal to the proportional split) as a benchmark and chose bids just above the likely clusters of other applicants on the high-value castles, giving up most of castles 1-2. For Game 2, a castle goes to the highest of four bids and first place pays far more than the others, so I picked a two-castle concentration: 8 points (castles 5+3) guarantees first, and 66/34 should beat nearly everyone on both. Both choices rest on guesses about what other applicants submit, so they are well-reasoned bets, not provably optimal answers.

Game 1 is scored by average points, so the castles are independent and the goal is to beat the most common opponent numbers per castle as cheaply as possible. I guessed at a likely field (even splits, proportional splits, 40-ish on castle 5, 30-35 on castle 4, 20 on castle 3, many zeros on castles 1-2) and placed soldiers one above those clusters. Game 2 is rank-based with a big reward for first, so I concentrated on castles 3 and 5, whose 8 combined points guarantee first. I put more on castle 5 to beat the obvious 50 and 60 bids and enough on castle 3 to beat typical 30-35 bids. Both choices depend on guesses about other entrants, so they are judgment calls rather than proven optima.

Neither game has an objectively optimal answer, so I guessed at what applicants typically submit (even splits, value-based splits, round numbers, dropping the low castles) and picked allocations that beat those. For Game 1, where points are averaged, I chose small margins over common values on castles 3-5 plus cheap wins on castles 1-2. For Game 2, being ranked in a 4-player group means you have to win castles outright, so I concentrated on castles 3 and 4 and left the contested castle 5 alone, since 7 points nearly always wins 1st. The main risk in Game 2 is that many others make the same contrarian move.

I assumed the field is mostly AI-generated entries that are roughly proportional and top-heavy, often with round or plus-one numbers, and tested candidates by hand against a made-up pool of such entries. For Game 1, conceding castle 5 (plus a 3-soldier token to beat other skip-5 entries) and beating typical amounts on castles 1-4 scored about 9.5 average, versus about 7.5 for a typical entry. For Game 2, the four-way format makes castles 4 and 5 very expensive, so securing castles 1-3 (6 points) with big margins gives 1st whenever castles 4 and 5 go to different opponents and usually 2nd otherwise. These are bets on opponent behavior, not guarantees, and if many people get similar advice the edge shrinks.

game2_bottom5.reasoning: Round numbers that climb with castle value.

Game 1 is a head-to-head Colonel Blotto style game with unknown opponents, and proportional allocation matches the average of the known equilibrium for weighted battlefields, so I used 7, 13, 20, 27, 33. Game 2 pays heavily for first place, so I concentrated on the high-value castles 4 and 5 and conceded castle 1 and much of castle 2, giving 5, 10, 20, 30, 35. I checked the second allocation informally against a proportional opponent and it came out ahead. The Game 2 choice is a heuristic, not a computed optimum, and it could be wrong if the other applicants are also top-heavy.
AI (sonnet) suggested 5/10/22/28/35; I added +1 to round numbers to win ties.

I treated Game 1 as a Colonel Blotto game against a mixed pool of naive players (even splits or value-proportional splits), so I conceded castles 1 and 2 and placed slightly above typical levels on castles 3, 4 and 5 to win 12 of 15 points against those players. For Game 2 the payout is rank-based and top-heavy, so I favored a concentrated allocation that is likely to win the three biggest castles, with a bit more on castles 4 and 5 because the maximum of three opponents is a tougher bar. These choices come from reasoning about likely opponent behavior, not from simulation, so there is real uncertainty.
